Outreach playbook

Start with permission and property facts. Keep the conversation clear and respectful.

First conversation

Adapt these examples to your role and local rules.

Phone opener

“Hi, I’m [your name]. I’m reaching out about the property at [address]. Are you the right person to speak with about the property? If you’d consider an as-is sale, I can ask a few questions and share a written offer. There’s no pressure, and you can take time to review it.”

Text message

“Hello, this is [your name]. Would you be open to discussing a possible purchase of [property address]? I can make an as-is offer after learning a little about the property. If this isn’t relevant, reply ‘no’ and I won’t follow up.”

Investor introduction

“I’m reviewing a property in [area]: [brief condition summary]. The estimated ARV is [amount], repairs are roughly [amount], and the verified source is [link/date]. Would it fit your current buy box? I can send the full deal sheet if you’re interested.”
Do not imply an official affiliation, guarantee a value, or use private case details as leverage. Respect do-not-contact requests. Check applicable federal, state, and local solicitation, real-estate licensing, privacy, and advertising rules before contacting sellers or investors.

Research checklist

Move from a public signal to a verified property lead.

  1. Find a property-level signal on an official or primary source.
  2. Confirm the address and current ownership through county property records.
  3. Record the source URL and date checked; note uncertainty.
  4. Estimate ARV from recent comparable sales and inspect repair assumptions.
  5. Confirm investor criteria and all transaction costs.
  6. Use a neutral introduction; stop if asked not to contact again.
  7. Document follow-up dates and keep only necessary business notes.
